One potential confounder is that the difference in survival of patients receiving ABT might be due to concurrent infections not present in the control group. To study this, we analyzed the cohort by administration route, assuming patients receiving intravenous ABT were more likely to be hospitalized than patients receiving oral ABT who were more likely to receive treatment as an outpatient. When assessing administration route (IV v PO v no ABT), ICI patients demonstrated a negative correlation with rwOS only among recipients of PO ABT (median: 36.2 v 23.5 v 33.6 months, P = .012), whereas rwOS was negatively affected by both routes in TKI recipients (median: 15.2 v 18.1 v 26.2 months, P < .001). Each treatment cohort demonstrated a reduced rwPFS (ICI median: 9.7 v 8.8 v 11.6 months, P = .002; TKI median: 6.4 v 8.2 v 9.7 months, P = .001; Fig 5).
